title: Latency: streaming, parallel calls, speculative work
story:
The number a user experiences is not the time your system takes. It is the time until something appears, and then whether the thing keeps appearing at a readable pace. Two systems with identical total times feel entirely different if one shows nothing for the whole duration and the other starts immediately. That gap is why streaming is the first thing to reach for: it does not make the work faster, it changes when the waiting becomes visible, and the waiting is what people report.

That said, perceived time is the first lever and not the only one, so measure the real path before optimising anything. Break the request into its stages — assembling context, retrieval, reranking, generation, whatever post-processing you do — and record each one separately. Without that breakdown, optimisation is guesswork, and the guess is usually wrong because the slow stage is rarely the interesting one.

When you do look at generation, note an asymmetry that decides where the time goes. The input is processed in one pass, while the output is produced one token after another, each depending on the one before. Output length is therefore serial time in a way input length is not, which makes the most reliable latency improvement available to you the unglamorous one: ask for less output. A shorter answer is faster in direct proportion, with no infrastructure involved.

Next, stop paying for sequence you did not need. Work that does not depend on other work should run at the same time — retrieval alongside a metadata lookup, several documents scored together, two independent tools called at once. Chains form by accident, because each step was added after the previous one and the code reads naturally that way, and the latency bill for that accident is paid on every request forever.

Speculative work is the lever after that, and it is a trade rather than a win. Start the likely work before you know you need it: retrieve while the user is still typing, begin generating from the top candidates while the rest are still being scored, prefetch the data the next step will probably want. When the guess is right you have saved the whole step. When it is wrong you have paid for work you threw away. That is worth doing exactly where time is scarcer than money, which is a judgement about your product, not a technique to apply everywhere.

Everything in the request path needs a timeout and a defined behaviour when it fires, and this is where latency work meets reliability work. Decide in advance what a degraded answer looks like — the retrieval order without reranking, the cached answer rather than the fresh one, an honest message rather than a spinner that never resolves. A system with no defined degraded mode does not avoid degrading; it simply degrades in whatever way the code happens to allow, at the worst possible moment.

And measure the distribution rather than the average. The average is comfortable and describes nobody: it hides the slow tail where users actually live, and the tail is what fills your queues, exhausts your connections and produces the complaints. A system whose typical response is quick and whose worst is unbounded will be remembered for the worst. Set a target at the tail, measure against it, and alert on it — the average will take care of itself.

problem.name: Time in the request path
problem.shape: A person is waiting, and the work has several stages of which only some are on the critical path.
tell: nothing appears until the whole answer is ready
stages run one after another though none depends on the last
the per-stage timings have never been recorded
the target is stated as an average
no stage has a timeout or a defined degraded result
problem.move: Stream so waiting becomes visible early, measure each stage separately, shorten the output because it is produced serially, run independent work concurrently, speculate only where time is scarcer than money, and give every stage a timeout with a defined degraded answer.
problem.invariant: The input is processed in one pass while the output is produced one token after another, so output length is serial time and shortening it shortens the response in direct proportion.
problem.breaks: Averages describe nobody — the tail is what fills queues, exhausts connections and generates complaints, so a target set on the mean leaves the real failure unmeasured.

cost.time: speculation spends compute on work that may be discarded, which is the price of starting before you know
cost.space: concurrency multiplies in-flight resources, so parallel stages raise peak memory and connection use
cost.beats: optimising the model choice, which addresses one stage of several, and doing nothing visible, which leaves the user watching a blank screen for the whole duration

problem.practice: Instrument each stage of one request path and print the timings for a hundred real requests, then sort by total and look at the slowest five. The stage that dominates there is almost never the one you would have optimised, and finding that out costs an hour.

beats.broke: Total time is optimised while the user waits on a blank screen, stages run in sequence out of habit, and the target is set on an average that describes nobody.
beats.fix: Stream so waiting starts visibly, measure per stage, shorten the serial output, run independent work concurrently, and give every stage a timeout with a defined degraded answer.
beats.cost: Speculation pays for discarded work and concurrency raises peak resource use, so both buy time with something else.

interview.q: What actually determines how slow one of these systems feels, and where should the work go?
interview.trap: Optimising total time while nothing appears on screen. Perceived latency is time to first output, so streaming changes the experience without changing the work — and then the real path still has to be measured per stage.
interview.answer:
Perceived time, which is the time until something appears and whether it keeps appearing. Two systems with the same total feel completely different if one shows nothing throughout, so streaming comes first — it changes when the waiting becomes visible rather than making anything faster.

Then I measure per stage: context assembly, retrieval, reranking, generation, post-processing. Without the breakdown, optimisation is guesswork and the slow stage is rarely the interesting one.

The asymmetry that decides where time goes is that the input is processed in one pass while the output is produced token by token, each depending on the last. Output length is serial time in a way input length is not, so the most reliable improvement is to ask for less output — it shortens in proportion with no infrastructure at all.

After that, stop paying for accidental sequence: anything independent should run concurrently, and chains form simply because steps were added in order. Speculative work — retrieving while the user types, generating from the top candidates while the rest are scored — is a trade of money for time, right only where time is the scarcer one.

Every stage needs a timeout and a defined degraded result, because a system without one still degrades, just unpredictably and at the worst moment. And I set targets on the tail rather than the average, since the tail is what fills queues, exhausts connections and produces the complaints.
